paragraphs.heading: The core equation
paragraphs.text: The Schrödinger equation is a partial differential equation. It governs the wave function of a quantum system that does not involve relativity. The wave function is the quantum description of an isolated system, and the equation says how it changes over time. Its discovery was a major landmark in the growth of quantum mechanics.

paragraphs.heading: Who and when
paragraphs.text: It is named after Erwin Schrödinger, an Austrian physicist. He postulated it in 1925 and published it in 1926, and it became the basis of the work that won him the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1933. He built it on Louis de Broglie's idea that all matter has a matter wave. The equation predicted the bound states of the atom, matching what experiments showed.

paragraphs.heading: Newton's law, quantum style
paragraphs.text: In concept, the equation does for quantum mechanics what Newton's second law does for classical mechanics. Newton's law starts from known initial conditions and predicts the path a system will follow over time. The Schrödinger equation instead predicts how the wave function evolves over time.

paragraphs.heading: The one-particle version
paragraphs.text: The simplest case is a single particle moving along one line, in position space. Its equation involves a wave function Ψ(x, t), giving a complex number for each point x at each time t. It also contains m, the particle's mass, and V(x, t), the potential energy that describes its surroundings. Two constants appear: i, the imaginary unit, and ℏ, the reduced Planck constant, whose units are energy multiplied by time. Introductory courses usually present the equation in a form like this, which can be followed with basic calculus alone.

paragraphs.heading: Putting it to work
paragraphs.text: To use the equation, you first write down the Hamiltonian, an expression that accounts for the kinetic and potential energies of the system's particles. You then insert it into the Schrödinger equation and solve for the wave function, which holds information about the system. In practice, the square of the wave function's absolute value at each point is treated as a probability density: Pr (x, t) = |Ψ(x, t)|².

paragraphs.heading: States and measurements
paragraphs.text: In the general theory, a system's state is a vector in a mathematical space called a complex Hilbert space, normalized so that ⟨ψ | ψ⟩ = 1. Measurable quantities such as position, momentum, energy and spin are represented by observables. A wave function that is an eigenvector of an observable is called an eigenstate, and its eigenvalue is the value the observable has in that state. In general a state is a linear combination of eigenstates, called a quantum superposition. A measurement gives one of the observable's eigenvalues, with a probability set by the Born rule.

paragraphs.heading: Other routes and limits
paragraphs.text: The equation is not the only way to do quantum mechanics: there is also Werner Heisenberg's matrix mechanics, and the path integral formulation, which was mainly the work of Richard Feynman. When these are compared, the Schrödinger approach is sometimes called wave mechanics. Schrödinger's equation is non-relativistic because it has a first derivative in time but a second derivative in space, so space and time are not on equal footing. Paul Dirac's equation, with a single derivative in both, joins special relativity and quantum mechanics and reduces to the Schrödinger equation in the non-relativistic limit.
